description: Tracked primary sources supporting the catalog anatomical capability model. A reference documents support; it is not a numeric muscle-contribution oracle.

sources.title: A model of the upper extremity for simulating musculoskeletal surgery and analyzing neuromuscular control
sources.scope: Upper-extremity musculotendon geometry and joint-crossing function.

sources.title: Moment arms of the muscles crossing the anatomical shoulder
sources.scope: Distinct moment arms for pectoralis-major, deltoid, rotator-cuff, latissimus-dorsi, and teres-major subregions.

sources.title: Muscle Contributions to Upper-Extremity Movement and Work From a Musculoskeletal Model of the Human Shoulder
sources.scope: Scapulothoracic musculoskeletal model tested against kinematics and surface EMG during shrugging plus unloaded and 2 kg loaded flexion and abduction in one healthy adult. Superior trapezius, serratus anterior, and deltoids showed the greatest activity and positive work during both loaded elevation paths; the single-subject model supports a categorical dynamic role, not population-level magnitude rankings.

sources.title: Associations between cervical and scapular posture and the spatial distribution of trapezius muscle activity
sources.scope: Functional recruitment differences across upper, middle, and lower trapezius subdivisions.

sources.title: Tendon Transfer Options for Trapezius Paralysis: A Biomechanical Study
sources.scope: Scapular rotation contributions involving trapezius, levator scapulae, and rhomboids.

sources.title: A model of the lower limb for analysis of human movement
sources.scope: A 44-compartment lower-limb musculoskeletal model based principally on architecture measured in 21 cadavers, with distinct paths and moment-generating functions for the rectus femoris and vasti; long- and short-head biceps femoris, medial hamstrings, gastrocnemii and soleus; iliacus, psoas, sartorius, adductors; and anterior, lateral, and deep lower-leg muscles across hip, knee, ankle, and foot position. It supports possible action capabilities, position-dependent moment-direction review, and the need to avoid false aggregate unions. It does not establish exercise-specific categorical roles; a whole-surface SceneKit mesh still cannot visualize modeled fiber or head subdivisions; and unconditioned profiles deliberately omit sagittal actions whose modeled direction changes across the admitted hip range.

sources.title: A musculoskeletal model for the lumbar spine
sources.scope: Lumbar muscle geometry, moment arms, and three-axis spinal motion.

sources.title: Non-uniform excitation of the pectoralis major muscle during flat and inclined bench press exercises
sources.scope: Regional pectoralis-major excitation during flat and 45-degree inclined barbell bench press, with the greatest flat-press amplitudes concentrated sternocostally.

sources.title: Specific prime movers' excitation during free-weight bench press variations and chest press machine in competitive bodybuilders
sources.scope: Clavicular and sternocostal pectoralis-major, triceps, and deltoid excitation during horizontal, inclined, and declined free-weight bench presses and a chest-press machine.

sources.title: A comparison of muscle activation between a Smith machine and free weight bench press
sources.scope: Pectoralis-major and deltoid excitation during free-weight and Smith-machine bench pressing at two relative loads.

sources.title: Comparison of Kinematics and Muscle Activation between Push-up and Bench Press
sources.scope: Kinematic and muscle-excitation comparison of loaded push-ups and bench presses across matched relative loads.

sources.title: Scapular kinematics and shoulder elevation in a traditional push-up
sources.scope: Three-dimensional scapular kinematics across elbow extension during traditional push-up variants.

sources.title: Kinetic analysis of several variations of push-ups
sources.scope: Ground-reaction-force estimates for standard, knee-supported, and hand- or foot-elevated push-up loading as fractions of body mass.

sources.title: Force direction and arm position affect contribution of clavicular and sternal parts of pectoralis major muscle during muscle strength testing
sources.scope: Regional pectoralis-major contribution under horizontal and positive or negative 30-degree oblique force directions relative to the transverse plane.

sources.title: Influence of bench angle on upper extremity muscular activation during bench press exercise
sources.scope: Regional pectoralis-major, anterior-deltoid, and triceps excitation across minus-15, flat, 30-degree, and 45-degree barbell bench pressing.

sources.title: Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise
sources.scope: Pectoralis-major regional, anterior-deltoid, and triceps excitation at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 degrees, including the clavicular maximum at 30 degrees and deltoid shift above 45 degrees.

sources.title: The Effects of Bench Press Variations in Competitive Athletes on Muscle Activity and Performance
sources.scope: Clavicular and sternocostal pectoralis-major, deltoid, triceps, biceps, and latissimus-dorsi excitation during 6-RM flat, plus-25-degree incline, and minus-25-degree decline barbell bench pressing in competitive athletes.

sources.title: Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row
sources.scope: Direction-specific rotator-cuff recruitment during bench pressing and rowing, including dynamic stabilization against anterior-posterior humeral-head translation and the row-specific subscapularis finding.

sources.title: Electromyographic analysis of scapula stabilizers muscles during the push up and bench press exercises in university athletes with and without shoulder impingement syndrome
sources.scope: Upper, middle, and lower trapezius and serratus-anterior excitation during push-up and flat bench-press tasks in university athletes with and without shoulder impingement syndrome.

sources.title: Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press
sources.scope: Serratus-anterior excitation and scapular-abduction excursion during flat barbell bench pressing and a chest-press lever machine at submaximal and 10-RM loading.

sources.title: Muscle function in glenohumeral joint stability during lifting task
sources.scope: Stability-constrained upper-limb simulation during a bimanual hip-to-shoulder lifting task, supporting a supraspinatus contribution to glenohumeral compression and reduced shear; not direct overhead-press role evidence.

sources.title: Kinematic characteristics of the scapula and clavicle during military press exercise and shoulder flexion
sources.scope: Scapular and clavicular kinematics in 16 healthy men during a light-load military press, including upward rotation and posterior tilt; the 2 kg load limits generalization to heavy pressing.

sources.title: Shoulder Muscle Activation of Novice and Resistance Trained Women during Variations of Dumbbell Press Exercises
sources.scope: Anterior-deltoid, clavicular- and sternal-pectoralis-major, and upper-trapezius excitation during 0-, 45-, and 85-degree bilateral dumbbell presses with 4.5 kg per hand in 24 healthy college-aged women; the fixed light load limits generalization to heavy pressing.

sources.title: Muscle activity of the core during bilateral, unilateral, seated and standing resistance exercise
sources.scope: Rectus-abdominis, external-oblique, and erector-spinae excitation across bilateral and unilateral neutral-grip dumbbell shoulder presses at 80% 1-RM in 15 healthy men; seated conditions used a 75-degree backrest supporting the upper torso and glutes.

sources.title: Effects of body position and loading modality on muscle activity and strength in shoulder presses
sources.scope: Anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoid, biceps, and triceps excitation plus one-repetition maximum across seated and standing barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses in 15 healthy men.

sources.title: Front vs Back and Barbell vs Machine Overhead Press: An Electromyographic Analysis and Implications For Resistance Training
sources.scope: Anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoid, upper-trapezius, pectoralis-major, and triceps excitation during front and behind-neck barbell and machine overhead presses in eight competitive male bodybuilders.

sources.title: Surface electromyography excitation in barbell vs. kettlebell overhead press prime movers and stabilizer muscles
sources.scope: Prime-mover and stabilizer excitation during 8-RM standing barbell and single-arm standard-orientation kettlebell overhead presses in ten experienced male instructors, including deltoids, triceps, upper trapezius, rectus abdominis, external oblique, and erector spinae.

sources.title: Load–velocity profiling in the military press exercise: Effects of gender and training
sources.scope: Load-velocity profiling during a seated Smith-machine military press in 26 men and 13 women, with a six-week training follow-up in 24 men. The pronated-grip upper-chest-to-full-extension protocol supports the seated fixed-path setup; it does not establish muscle-role rankings.

sources.title: Surface electromyographic activation patterns and elbow joint motion during a pull-up, chin-up, or Perfect-Pullup rotational exercise
sources.scope: Surface-EMG and elbow-motion comparison of pull-ups, chin-ups, and a rotating-handle pull-up in 25 participants. It supports the pull-up/chin-up role envelope and grip-dependent differences, not continuous muscle weights.

sources.title: Kinematic and electromyographic comparisons between chin-ups and lat-pull down exercises
sources.scope: Direct kinematic and surface-EMG comparison of closed-chain chin-ups and open-chain lat pulldowns, supporting their shared movement family while preserving chain and body-position differences.

sources.title: Grip Width and Forearm Orientation Effects on Muscle Activity During the Lat Pull-Down
sources.scope: Latissimus-dorsi and elbow-flexor surface EMG during anterior lat pulldowns using pronated and supinated orientations and different grip widths in 12 trained men at 70% one-repetition maximum.

sources.title: Effects of Grip Width on Muscle Strength and Activation in the Lat Pull-Down
sources.scope: Six-repetition-maximum strength and surface EMG during pronated lat pulldowns at 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 times biacromial grip width in 15 men; the widths are authoring anchors rather than biological thresholds.

sources.title: Scapula kinematics of pull-up techniques: Avoiding impingement risk with training changes
sources.scope: Humerothoracic, glenohumeral, and scapulothoracic kinematics across three pull-up techniques in 11 trained participants. It supports explicit grip and scapular-motion modeling; its injury-risk interpretation is not used as a catalog prohibition.

sources.title: High-Density Electromyography Excitation in Front vs. Back Lat Pull-Down Prime Movers
sources.scope: High-density EMG comparison of front and behind-neck lat pulldowns at an eight-repetition-maximum load in 14 resistance-trained men. It supports the visible front-path boundary and exercise-specific secondary roles without making a universal safety claim.

sources.title: Scapular kinematics and task specificity: The effect of load direction
sources.scope: Biplanar-videoradiography comparison of loaded shoulder adduction and abduction in 10 healthy adults. Orientation differences and participant variability caution against inferring scapular rotation direction from arm travel alone.

sources.title: Electromyographic Analysis of Back Muscle Activation During Lat Pulldown Exercise: Effects of Grip Variations and Forearm Orientation
sources.scope: Surface EMG of latissimus dorsi, posterior deltoid, biceps, middle and lower trapezius, and infraspinatus across seven bilateral front-pulldown grip, width, and torso-angle conditions in 40 trained men; no unilateral condition was tested.

sources.title: Alterations in kinematics and muscle activation patterns with the addition of a kipping action during a pull-up activity
sources.scope: Kinematics and surface EMG during strict and kipping pull-ups in 11 athletes. The substantially greater hip, knee, trunk, and lower-body contribution supports keeping kipping outside the strict vertical-pull contract.

sources.title: A Comparison of Muscle Activation during the Pull-up and Three Alternative Pulling Exercises
sources.scope: Surface-EMG comparison of bodyweight pull-ups, seated and kneeling lat pulldowns, and an assisted pull-up condition. It supports assisted-machine coverage but does not isolate a supinated assisted chin-up.

sources.title: Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: An experimental study
sources.scope: Surface EMG during traditional latissimus-dorsi exercises in 12 trained participants, including seated rows with latissimus dorsi, biceps, and a combined middle-trapezius/rhomboid electrode site. The combined site cannot apportion the two retractors independently.

sources.title: Comparison of Different Rowing Exercises: Trunk Muscle Activation and Lumbar Spine Motion, Load, and Stiffness
sources.scope: Trunk EMG, lumbar motion, load, and stiffness in seven men during inverted, bent-over, and one-arm cable rows. It supports explicit position-specific spinal demands rather than one universal row-stability assignment.

sources.title: The Effect of Performing Bi- and Unilateral Row Exercises on Core Muscle Activation
sources.scope: Surface EMG in 15 resistance-trained men during bilateral and unilateral free-weight bent-over, seated cable, and machine rows. Unilateral conditions increased external-oblique excitation, while trunk-extensor demand varied by equipment and laterality.

sources.title: Activation of Spinal Stabilizers and Shoulder Complex Muscles During an Inverted Row Using a Portable Pull-up Device and Body Weight Resistance
sources.scope: Shoulder-complex and spinal-stabilizer surface EMG during a bodyweight inverted row in 26 participants. It supports the admitted inverted-row muscle envelope without establishing one universal effective-bodyweight fraction.

sources.title: Recruitment of Shoulder Complex and Torso Stabilizer Muscles With Rowing Exercises Using a Suspension Strap Training System
sources.scope: Surface EMG in 28 participants across low, high, and horizontal-abduction suspension rows. Distinct excitation profiles support separating shoulder-extension rows from flared horizontal-abduction rows; the article appeared online in 2020 and in the 2021 journal issue.

sources.title: Shoulder Retractor Strengthening Exercise to Minimize Rhomboid Muscle Activity and Subacromial Impingement
sources.scope: Fine-wire EMG recruited 12 participants and reports analyzable data from 8, confirming middle-trapezius and rhomboid coactivation in a 90-degree-abducted, elbow-flexed rowing position. The static rehabilitation task is directly relevant to the shoulder-height-row family but does not establish dynamic loaded roles across its roster or the narrow/tucked shoulder-extension-row variants.

sources.title: Can different variations of suspension exercises provide adequate loads and muscle activations for upper body training?
sources.scope: Applied strap forces and surface EMG across suspension-exercise setups in 12 male athletes. Setup- and phase-dependent loading supports a pinned inverted-row geometry and cautions against one bodyweight fraction for every inclination.

sources.title: High-Density Surface Electromyography Excitation of Prime Movers in the Narrow vs. Wide Grip Seated Row Exercise
sources.scope: High-density surface EMG in 14 trained men comparing narrow and wide seated rows. The wide setup increased trapezius and lateral-deltoid excitation while the narrow setup increased latissimus excitation, supporting an upper-arm-path boundary without establishing a 90-degree shoulder-height row; grip width, pull target, and humeral path covaried.

sources.title: High-Density Surface Electromyography Excitation of Prime Movers Across Scapular Positions in the Seated Row
sources.scope: High-density surface EMG in 14 trained men comparing deliberately fixed and free scapular seated-row techniques at 8-RM. It supports a visible technique boundary but does not make an anterior chest pad equivalent to fixed scapular translation; the article appeared online in December 2025 and in the 2026 issue.

sources.title: Electromyographical responses of the lumbar, dorsal and shoulder musculature during the bent-over row exercise: a comparison between standing and bench postures (a preliminary study)
sources.scope: Preliminary surface-EMG comparison of standing and inclined-bench bent-over rows with adducted and 90-degree-abducted upper-arm paths in only three participants. It informs posture and support vocabulary but is not load-bearing evidence for a muscle-role change.

sources.title: Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row
authors: Christine Megumi Wakuda de Abreu Vasconcelos
sources.scope: Peak cable force and surface EMG in 21 recreationally trained adults across pronated, supinated, and neutral grip conditions described as nearer 0 degrees, plus separately named 30-, 60-, and 90-degree shoulder-abduction conditions. Greater abduction shifted excitation toward upper and middle trapezius and posterior deltoid and away from upper and lower latissimus while reducing peak force; grip setup and humeral path covaried, and the dynamic load was derived from the pronated condition.

sources.title: Shoulder-Abduction Angle and Trapezius Muscle Activity During Scapular-Retraction Exercise
sources.scope: Surface EMG in 35 asymptomatic participants during elastic-resistance scapular retraction at 0, 45, 90, and 120 degrees of shoulder abduction; only the isometric phase was analyzed. The 90-degree condition produced the highest overall trapezius excitation, but lower-trapezius activity remained below upper and middle trapezius and did not differ significantly between 0 and 90 degrees; the rehabilitation load and diagonal 120-degree condition are not condition-matched heavy-row evidence.

sources.title: Effects of different movement directions on electromyography recorded from the shoulder muscles while passing the target positions
sources.scope: Fine-wire supraspinatus and surface infraspinatus and deltoid EMG in 15 healthy untrained men during controlled elevation, depression, horizontal adduction, and horizontal abduction through matched target positions. It supports direction-sensitive cuff and deltoid recruitment during horizontal abduction, not a mandatory cuff role in a loaded compound row.

sources.title: Effects of the pullover exercise on the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi muscles as evaluated by EMG
sources.scope: Surface EMG in eight healthy men during loaded barbell pullovers. Pectoralis-major excitation exceeded latissimus-dorsi excitation in this free-weight setup; the result is exercise- and resistance-profile-specific rather than a universal pullover hierarchy.

sources.title: Comparison of Electromyographic Activity during Barbell Pullover and Straight Arm Pulldown Exercises
sources.scope: Surface-EMG comparison of a barbell pullover at 100% biacromial hand spacing with straight-arm cable pulldowns at 100% and 150% biacromial spacing. It supports treating free-weight pullovers and cable straight-arm pulldowns as distinct resistance-profile branches while retaining a common shoulder-extension action.

sources.title: Muscle Activity in Upper-Body Single-Joint Resistance Exercises with Elastic Resistance Bands vs. Free Weights
sources.scope: Matched 10-RM surface-EMG comparison of elastic-band and dumbbell flyes and reverse flyes in 29 adults. It supports both implements as reviewed single-joint variants while documenting phase- and implement-dependent excitation rather than interchangeable muscle magnitudes.

sources.title: Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major and Anterior Deltoid Muscles During Three Upper-Body Lifts
sources.scope: Pectoralis-major and anterior-deltoid surface EMG during the concentric phase of 6-RM barbell bench press, dumbbell bench press, and dumbbell fly in 12 adults. It directly anchors the dumbbell-fly roster but does not resolve regional pectoralis-major excitation.

sources.title: Effect of Hand Position on EMG Activity of the Posterior Shoulder Musculature During a Horizontal Abduction Exercise
sources.scope: Posterior-deltoid and infraspinatus surface EMG during reverse-fly-machine horizontal abduction with neutral and pronated hand positions. It supports both reviewed grip fixtures and their posterior-shoulder role envelope, not a separate external-rotation prime action.

sources.title: Motion of the Shoulder Complex During Multiplanar Humeral Elevation
sources.scope: Bone-pin three-dimensional shoulder-complex kinematics in 12 healthy adults during sagittal flexion, scapular-plane elevation, and coronal abduction. It supports coupled scapular upward rotation and posterior tilt during elevation without assigning fixed magnitudes to loaded raises.

sources.title: The Muscle Functions Around the Scapula During Clavicle-Glenohumeral Rhythm in the Motion of Shoulder Flexion and Abduction
sources.scope: Upper-, middle-, and lower-trapezius plus serratus-anterior surface EMG at six static positions (0, 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 degrees) during unweighted flexion and abduction in six healthy volunteers. Upper-trapezius activity increased gradually in both paths; the reported early path differences instead involved greater serratus-anterior and lower-trapezius activity in flexion and greater middle-trapezius activity in abduction. The small held-position study supports common upper-trapezius recruitment, not an exact loaded-role ranking or equal magnitude between raise families.

sources.title: Shoulder- and Back-Muscle Activation During Shoulder Abduction and Flexion Using a Bodyblade Pro Versus Dumbbells
sources.scope: Deltoid, pectoralis-major, infraspinatus, serratus-anterior, and erector-spinae surface EMG near 90 degrees during dumbbell shoulder flexion and abduction at three light loads in 11 healthy men. It anchors dumbbell raise fixtures but not an exact muscle-role ranking across the full range.

sources.title: Deltoid muscle contribution to shoulder flexion and abduction strength: an experimental approach
sources.scope: Shoulder flexion and abduction strength before and after axillary-nerve block in 12 healthy adults. It establishes a substantial deltoid contribution that increases with elevation, while whole-deltoid measurement requires moment-arm evidence for subregion-specific family roles.

sources.title: Dumbbell versus cable lateral raises for lateral deltoid hypertrophy: an experimental study
sources.scope: Within-person training comparison of unilateral dumbbell and cable lateral raises from the arm-at-side start to 90 degrees with an extended elbow. The prescribed path was frontal except for consistent symptom-driven scapular-plane accommodations in some participants; those accommodations do not admit scaption into the strict family.

sources.title: Shoulder Muscle Recruitment Patterns During Commonly Used Rotator Cuff Exercises: An Electromyographic Study
sources.scope: Fine-wire and surface EMG in 15 healthy adults during low-, medium-, and high-intensity pulley-resisted internal and external rotation with the arm by the side. It directly anchors dynamic at-side cable fixtures and shows graded recruitment across torque-capable muscles rather than one muscle acting alone.

sources.title: Electromyographic Analysis of the Rotator Cuff and Deltoid Musculature During Common Shoulder External Rotation Exercises
sources.scope: Intramuscular rotator-cuff and deltoid EMG in 10 healthy adults across seven external-rotation exercise positions, including standing and side-lying at zero abduction and prone or standing at 90 degrees. It supports the reviewed external-rotation positions while leaving load-path and support mechanics explicit in the roster.

sources.title: Is subscapularis recruited in a similar manner during shoulder internal rotation exercises and belly press and lift off tests?
sources.scope: Intramuscular subscapularis EMG during maximal isometric internal-rotation tasks at zero and 90 degrees of abduction and during clinical test positions. It supports subscapularis capability and position review but is not direct evidence for a dynamic cable or band trajectory.

sources.title: Electromyographic Activity and Applied Load During Shoulder Rehabilitation Exercises Using Elastic Resistance
sources.scope: Fine-wire and surface EMG with applied-load measurement in 19 healthy men during controlled elastic-resistance shoulder exercises, including dynamic internal and external rotation. It directly anchors low-load band fixtures without implying equivalence to cable resistance.

sources.title: Variation of muscle moment arms with elbow and forearm position
sources.scope: Cadaveric tendon-excursion measurements of elbow-flexion and forearm-rotation moment arms across elbow and forearm positions. It distinguishes the mechanical capabilities of biceps brachii, brachialis, brachioradialis, pronator teres, and triceps, but does not establish exercise-level activation or training emphasis.

sources.title: Moment arms of forearm rotators
sources.scope: Tendon excursions on an epoxy radioulnar model, verified on one fresh cadaver specimen, across the full forearm-rotation range at three elbow angles. It supports unconditional pronator and supinator moment directions and brachioradialis return toward neutral, not in-vivo exercise roles or contribution magnitudes.

sources.title: The function of brachioradialis
sources.scope: Fine-wire EMG in ten healthy adults during loaded elbow flexion and rotation from full pronation or supination toward neutral. It supports elbow flexion as the consistent function and a secondary rotational role, not unconditional full-range pronation or supination.

sources.title: Electromyographic activity and strength during maximum isometric pronation and supination efforts in healthy adults
sources.scope: Fine-wire EMG and torque in fourteen healthy adults during maximum isometric pronation and supination at five forearm positions without gripping. It supports pronator-teres and pronator-quadratus contribution to pronation and supinator and biceps contribution to supination, not dynamic exercise trajectories or submaximal role rankings.

sources.title: Wrist tendon moment arms: Quantification by imaging and experimental techniques
sources.scope: MRI-derived and tendon-excursion measurements in ten cadaveric upper limbs for FCR, FCU, ECRL, ECRB, ECU, and APL about wrist flexion-extension and radioulnar-deviation axes. Differences between methods for some tendons bound its use to categorical wrist actions rather than universal moment-arm magnitudes.

sources.title: Wrist salvage procedures alter moment arms of the primary wrist muscles
sources.scope: Tendon-excursion measurements in eight cadaveric specimens across flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation before and after two wrist-salvage procedures. The nonimpaired measurements independently confirm the categorical antagonist sets; the surgical comparisons do not define healthy exercise contribution magnitudes.

sources.title: Tendon excursion and moment arm of index finger muscles
sources.scope: Tendon-excursion measurements across individual index-finger flexion-extension and abduction-adduction ranges, with moment arms derived relative to joint centers. It supports categorical extrinsic finger-flexor and finger-extensor actions, not whole-hand grip tasks or exercise-level recruitment.

sources.title: A musculoskeletal model of the hand and wrist: model definition and evaluation
sources.scope: A 43-muscle OpenSim hand-wrist model built from one cadaveric dataset and evaluated against published index-finger and wrist moment arms plus static pinch forces. It supports coherent finger-wrist capability mapping, not population-level force estimates or dynamic training roles.

sources.title: Exploring forearm muscle coordination and training applications of various grip positions during maximal isometric finger dead-hangs in rock climbers
sources.scope: Surface EMG of FDP, FDS, FCR, and EDC in twenty-five climbers during maximal isometric dead-hangs using three climbing-specific grip positions. It supports loaded finger-flexor recruitment and wrist-muscle co-contraction in static support, but does not by itself admit a dynamic gripper, pinch, or generic grip family.

sources.title: A mechanical study of the moment-forces of the supinators and pronators of the forearm
sources.scope: Cadaveric torque across forearm rotation in eight specimens with the elbow fixed at 90 degrees. It supports biceps and supinator supination, pronator-teres and pronator-quadratus pronation, and position-dependent torque; it is not exercise EMG or a product-load prescription.

sources.title: Effect of 12 Weeks of Wrist and Forearm Training on High School Baseball Players
sources.scope: Twelve-week wrist and forearm program in male high-school baseball players using barbell wrist flexion and extension plus resisted pronation, supination, and radial-ulnar deviation. It anchors the loaded exercise directions and 8-to-12-repetition programming, not adult-generalized seed weights or individual-muscle roles; detailed testing used laboratory restraint that the catalog adapts to coached free setups.

sources.title: Flexor-Pronator Mass Training Exercises Selectively Activate Forearm Musculature
sources.scope: Dynamic elastic-band pronation and ulnar-deviation protocols in ten healthy men measured pronator teres, FDS, and FCU only. It supports a conservative role envelope but neither its full-range pronation nor shoulder-height ulnar-deviation setup is copied into the narrow offset-dumbbell roster; unmeasured muscles cannot be ranked inactive.

sources.title: Characterizing forearm muscle activity in young adults during dynamic wrist flexion-extension movement using a wrist robot
sources.scope: Dynamic wrist flexion-extension in twelve young men across forearm orientations with an instrumented wrist robot and an eight-muscle EMG panel. It supports phase-dependent wrist-mover and co-contraction roles, not equivalence between the robot handle and the catalog's barbell fixture.

sources.title: Characterizing forearm muscle activity in university-aged males during dynamic radial-ulnar deviation of the wrist using a wrist robot
sources.scope: Dynamic radial-ulnar deviation in twelve university-aged men across forearm orientations with an instrumented wrist robot and surface EMG. It supports multi-muscle, direction- and phase-dependent deviation roles, not free-weight equivalence or numeric involvement weights.

sources.title: Biceps Brachii and Brachioradialis Excitation in Biceps Curl Exercise: Different Handgrips, Different Synergy
sources.scope: Ten competitive male bodybuilders performed strict bilateral cable curls using a straight bar for supinated and pronated conditions and a rope for neutral. It directly anchors those fixtures and relative excitation, but brachialis was not measured and EMG is not a numeric contribution or hypertrophy oracle.

sources.title: Muscular coordination of biceps brachii and brachioradialis in elbow flexion with respect to hand position
sources.scope: Sixteen participants performed repeated controlled elbow flexion in three forearm positions at 20 degrees per second. Its pronated brachioradialis finding bounds the categorical role policy, while its loading and task differ from heavy cable curls and conflict with Coratella's orientation ordering.

sources.title: Effect of shoulder position on triceps brachii heads activity in dumbbell elbow extension exercises
sources.scope: Twenty-one trained men performed unilateral seated-overhead and supine-90-degree dumbbell elbow extensions at 40 percent MVIC. The study directly anchors the two postures but measured only the long and lateral triceps heads and does not establish product seed weights or a hypertrophy hierarchy.

sources.title: Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position
sources.scope: Issue-year 2023 study published online in 2022: twenty-one adults trained unilateral standing cable elbow extension for twelve weeks with the shoulder fixed at 180 versus 0 degrees and a supinated wrist. It anchors posture and aggregate adaptation, not separate app roles for triceps heads or other grips; it does not report the cable attachment, pulley height, anchor setting, or cable angle.

sources.title: Forearm Position Influences Triceps Brachii Activation During Triceps Push-Down Exercise
sources.scope: Twenty-two adults performed single-arm pronated and supinated pushdowns with a handle or padded strap. It supports those reviewed variants and observed radial wrist-flexor/extensor stabilization; the same-absolute-load maximal-repetition design and attachment mechanics limit triceps ranking and provide no longitudinal outcome.

sources.title: Serratus anterior or pectoralis minor: Which muscle has the upper hand during protraction exercises?
sources.scope: Twenty-six participants performed a serratus punch plus wall and floor modified push-up-plus conditions while serratus anterior surface EMG and pectoralis-minor fine-wire EMG were recorded. Serratus activity was significantly greater than pectoralis-minor activity during the punch; the study supports their categorical roles in a protraction task, not numeric contribution weights or unmeasured scapular rotations and tilts.

sources.title: Supine scapular punch: An exercise for early phases of shoulder rehabilitation?
sources.scope: Supine scapular-punch surface EMG in healthy volunteers and participants with unilateral shoulder pain found moderate-to-high serratus-anterior activity with very low upper-trapezius and infraspinatus activity. It directly anchors the exercise setup and conservative target emphasis, but it does not supply three-dimensional scapular kinematics or justify a numeric role hierarchy.

sources.title: Modifying the shoulder joint position during shrugging and retraction exercises alters the activation of the medial scapular muscles
sources.scope: Surface and fine-wire EMG compared upper trapezius, levator scapulae, middle and lower trapezius, and rhomboid major across loaded shrug and retraction positions. It supports a narrow loaded shrug role envelope and position sensitivity; it did not measure scapular kinematics, so the coupled upward-rotation action comes from the separately cited shrug model rather than this EMG study.

sources.title: Bench, Bar, and Ring Dips: Do Kinematics and Muscle Activity Differ?
sources.scope: Thirteen experienced men performed bench, parallel-bar, and ring dips with three-dimensional kinematics and a nine-muscle surface-EMG panel. It directly anchors the two admitted suspended fixtures, shoulder-extension bottom position, concentric shoulder-flexion and elbow-extension boundary, and apparatus-conditioned activity; raw within-muscle EMG cannot rank different muscles, and scapular kinematics were not measured.

sources.title: Fatigue Increases Muscle Activations but Does Not Change Maximal Joint Angles during the Bar Dip
sources.scope: Fifteen experienced men performed a parallel-bar dip set to exhaustion with three-dimensional kinematics and nine-muscle surface EMG. It confirms the shoulder-extended bottom and target-muscle activity across fatigue while explicitly leaving scapular kinematics unmeasured; it does not establish a whole-pectoralis or between-muscle force ranking.

sources.title: Effect of Elbow Angle on Triceps Brachii and Pectoralis Major Muscle Activity during Parallel Bar Dip
sources.scope: Ten exercise-trained men performed metronome-controlled parallel-bar dips to 75-, 85-, and 95-degree elbow angles while surface EMG sampled pectoralis major at the sternocostal-site placement midway from the sternal notch to the axillary fold. Pectoral excitation exceeded 38 percent MVC in every concentric condition and was greatest in the concentric phase. Combined with McKenzie's separately measured extended-bottom-to-neutral flexion path, the regional concentric signal provides a triangulated, exercise-specific basis for the catalog's narrowly conditioned capability and dip role; neither study directly measured sternocostal flexion torque. This study did not track shoulder, trunk, or scapular kinematics, distinguish sternocostal subregions, compare pectoral heads, establish a between-muscle force ranking, or directly study rings.

sources.title: Rehabilitation After Surgical Treatment of Pectoralis Major Rupture in a CrossFit Practitioner: A Case Report
sources.scope: A single trained man sustained a complete rupture of the pectoralis-major sternal portion during the loaded eccentric phase of a ring dip performed with 40 kilograms of added load. The case corroborates material sternocostal tissue loading on rings, but it cannot establish normal concentric recruitment, a shoulder-action capability, a categorical role, a between-region hierarchy, or an unweighted exercise prescription.

sources.title: Comparison of Joint Kinetics during Free Weight and Flywheel Resistance Exercise
sources.scope: Eleven trained men and women performed instrumented free-weight and flywheel front squats, lunges, and push presses. Joint-resolved impulse findings directly support knee-extension, hip-extension, and ankle-plantarflexion demands in the push press; they do not establish a categorical individual-muscle hierarchy or scapular actions.

sources.title: Power and Impulse Applied During Push Press Exercise
sources.scope: Seventeen resistance-trained men performed barbell push presses across 10 to 90 percent of one-repetition maximum on a force platform. It supports the front-rack task, lower-body countermovement and propulsion, overhead lockout, power modality, and low-repetition programming; it does not provide joint-resolved moments, scapular kinematics, or a complete muscle-role panel.

sources.title: Kinetics and Kinematics of the Push Press, Push Jerk, and Split Jerk
sources.scope: Eighteen resistance-trained men performed push presses, push jerks, and split jerks at 60, 75, and 90 percent of exercise one-repetition maximum. Force-time and task data support continuous foot contact, a single countermovement-propulsion phase, and standing lockout without a receiving dip as the push-press boundary; the study does not provide joint-resolved lower-limb moments, scapular kinematics, or a muscle-role hierarchy.

sources.title: The effects of hip flexion angle on quadriceps femoris muscle hypertrophy in the leg extension exercise
sources.scope: Direct unilateral 40- versus 90-degree hip-flexion leg-extension training with region-specific quadriceps hypertrophy outcomes. It supports the two fixture geometries and posture-sensitive rectus-femoris credit, not unmeasured vasti-head ranking, intermediate hip angles, bilateral variants, or universal machine-stack seeds. The 2025 issue article was published online on 2024-12-19.

sources.title: Hip flexion angle affects longitudinal muscle activity of the rectus femoris in leg extension exercise
sources.scope: Acute four-set isotonic machine leg extension at 70 percent one-repetition maximum with MRI T2 assessment at 0, 40, and 80 degrees of hip flexion. It supports longitudinal rectus-femoris hip-angle sensitivity, not long-term hypertrophy, other quadriceps-head roles, or permission for an 80-degree catalog fixture.

sources.title: Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths
sources.scope: Direct unilateral seated 90-degree versus prone 30-degree hip-flexion leg-curl training through 0 to 90 degrees of knee motion with pelvis straps and individual hamstring, sartorius, and gracilis MRI volumes. It supports the two fixtures and their categorical knee-flexor roles; ankle posture was not reported and calf involvement was not measured.

sources.title: Examining the Role of the Gastrocnemius during the Leg Curl Exercise
sources.scope: Maximal isokinetic knee flexions with the ankle braced in full dorsiflexion or plantarflexion plus a gastrocnemius model. It establishes that ankle posture is load-bearing for gastrocnemius contribution to knee flexion, not a categorical gastrocnemius role on the ankle-unreported Maeo weight-stack fixtures.

sources.title: Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training
sources.scope: Direct unilateral machine standing knee-extended versus seated knee-90-degree calf-raise training with neutral feet and individual gastrocnemius and soleus MRI volumes. It supports posture-dependent categorical credit, not a universal machine-stack seed or exact user range-of-motion endpoints.

sources.title: Comparison of gluteus maximus and hamstring electromyographic activity and lumbopelvic motion during three different prone hip extension exercises in healthy volunteers
sources.scope: Sixteen healthy men performed conventional prone, prone-table, and 90-degree-knee-flexed prone-table hip extension. Surface EMG measured gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and erector spinae while electromagnetic tracking measured pelvic rotation and anterior tilt. It supports the one reviewed bent-knee fixture and conservative categorical roles, not other apparatus, external loading, bilateral variants, or a zero-pelvic-motion claim.

sources.title: An investigation of movement dynamics and muscle activity during traditional and accentuated-eccentric squatting
sources.scope: The primary cohort comprised nine trained men performing motorized-cable traditional and accentuated-eccentric squats, while a secondary cohort directly compared barbell back, barbell front, and Kineo squats at 50, 85, and 100 percent body mass with lower-limb kinematics and gluteus-maximus and vastus-lateralis EMG. It supports front/back ankle-range transfer; it does not provide a complete muscle-policy ranking, a precise back-bar placement, or permission to activate the Kineo fixture.

sources.title: Biomechanical comparisons of back and front squats with a straight bar and four squats with a transformer bar
sources.scope: Eighteen trained adults performed hip-width straight-bar front and back squats plus four transformer-bar conditions at 70 percent of straight-bar front-squat one-repetition maximum. Estimated parallel-position trunk, pelvis, hip, knee, and ankle kinematics and kinetics directly support the two reviewed load placements; the study contains no exercise EMG and does not establish a fixed universal muscle-role ranking. The 2024 issue article was published online in 2020.

sources.title: Activity of Trunk and Lower Extremity Musculature: Comparison Between Parallel Back Squats and Belt Squats
sources.scope: Ten experienced participants performed three sets of five parallel back squats and belt squats with an external load equal to body mass while trunk and lower-extremity surface EMG was recorded. It directly supports the reviewed back-squat muscle panel and supplies an adverse belt-squat comparison; it contains no front-squat condition or kinematic equivalence analysis and cannot activate a belt-loaded branch.

sources.title: Effects of squat training with different depths on lower limb muscle volumes
sources.scope: A ten-week MRI intervention compared full- and half-squat training effects on lower-limb muscle volumes. It supports practical squat training-emphasis decisions and establishes depth sensitivity; group-level adductor findings cannot override the visible-region action model, prove equal compartment contributions, or activate an additional range-of-motion value.

sources.title: The Effect of Volitional Preemptive Abdominal Contraction on Biomechanical Measures During A Front Versus Back Loaded Barbell Squat
sources.scope: Twenty-six men performed loaded hip-width back and front squats to near-parallel depth with lumbar and lower-limb kinematics plus trunk and lower-limb surface EMG. It supports explicit trunk bracing and the two reviewed load placements; the deliberately lower front-squat load prevents a numeric cross-variant muscle ranking.

sources.title: Differences in hip, knee, and ankle joint moments during squats across load intensities, gender classes, and performance level in elite powerlifters
sources.scope: Twenty-nine elite powerlifters performed IPF-style low-bar squats at 70, 80, and 90 percent of estimated one-repetition maximum. Separate ankle-angle and joint-moment waveforms and the reported concentric plantarflexion support only the cross-squat ankle-action gate; the source does not activate a distinct low-bar record or define roles for the canonical back- and front-squat fixtures.

sources.title: Two-Experiment Examination of Habitual and Manipulated Foot Placement Angles on the Kinetics, Kinematics, and Muscle Forces of the Barbell Back Squat in Male Lifters
sources.scope: Two barbell-back-squat experiments examined habitual and manipulated foot-placement angles in male lifters at 70 percent one-repetition maximum using three-dimensional kinematics, kinetics, and modeled muscle forces. Gastrocnemius and soleus force estimates support plantarflexor contribution and show that foot angle is anatomy-bearing; the source does not pre-authorize a foot-orientation axis in the narrow roster.

sources.title: Kinematic and EMG activities during front and back squat variations in maximum loads
sources.scope: Twelve trained participants performed maximal front and back squats while knee kinematics and surface EMG of the vasti, rectus femoris, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae were recorded. It directly supports the medial-hamstring excitation contrast; surface EMG cannot establish net hip-extension contribution, so the active contract credits stabilization rather than dynamic work.

sources.title: A comprehensive biomechanical analysis of the barbell hip thrust
sources.scope: Nineteen resistance-trained men performed three barbell hip-thrust repetitions at 70 percent one-repetition maximum with three-dimensional kinematics and force plates under both feet and the thorax support. It supports hip and knee extension, dominant hip-extensor demand, free bar path, observed but nonstandardized ankle motion, and variable pelvic-trunk excursion; it supplies no muscle-specific EMG, bridge fixture, or zero-motion spine or ankle claim.

sources.title: Electromyographic differences of the gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis between the barbell hip thrust and barbell glute bridge
sources.scope: Ten trained men performed five-repetition-maximum barbell hip thrusts and glute bridges with standardized shoulder-width feet, a 35.5-centimeter thrust bench, 90-degree thrust endpoint, 135-degree bridge starting knee angle, approximately 115-degree bridge endpoint knee flexion, floor-versus-bench torso anchors, padded pelvic bar placement, supinated stabilizing grip, and hip-neutral endpoint. Knee angles use the study's flexion convention. Upper and lower gluteus-maximus, gluteus medius, biceps femoris, and vastus-lateralis EMG support the two fixtures and their categorical roles, not bodyweight, unilateral, machine, or band variants or precise spinal kinematics. The 2024 issue article was published online in 2022.

sources.title: Effects of step lengths on biomechanical characteristics of lower extremity during split squat movement
sources.scope: Twenty male college students performed barbell split squats at 50, 70, 100, and 120 percent of greater-trochanter-to-lateral-malleolus leg length while lead-limb kinematics, kinetics, and eight-muscle surface EMG were collected. The instructed erect torso, approximately parallel lead thigh, fixed split stance, and 100-percent condition anchor the reviewed motion and its lead-limb role envelope; posterior-limb loading was not collected, so the source establishes neither zero rear contribution nor a lead-dominant or percentage load split. The method also does not textually specify a stance landmark, bar site, or grip or activate other stance lengths, dynamic lunges, elevated feet, or other equipment.

sources.title: Does the Dumbbell-Carrying Position Change the Muscle Activity in Split Squats and Walking Lunges?
sources.scope: Fourteen resistance-trained and fourteen non-resistance-trained participants performed five-repetition-maximum split squats and forward walking lunges with ipsilateral or contralateral dumbbell carrying. Hip and knee range of motion plus gluteus-medius, vastus-medialis, vastus-lateralis, and biceps-femoris surface EMG support the stationary split-squat versus walking-lunge boundary and unilateral stabilization context; the source does not test the active straight-bar placement or prove equivalent roles across implements.

sources.title: Electromyographical Analysis of Lower Extremity Muscle Activation During Variations of the Loaded Step-Up Exercise
sources.scope: Fifteen resistance-trained women performed loaded forward, crossover, diagonal, and lateral step-ups at six-repetition-maximum loads on a 45.72-centimeter box while seven lower-extremity muscles were measured with surface EMG. It supports forward step-up action and muscle-role context and establishes that directional variants are not automatic synonyms; the publication does not report an external-load implement or placement and cannot anchor the active 21-centimeter bodyweight fixture, its load semantics, or its exact geometry.

sources.title: Lower-extremity biomechanics during forward and lateral stepping activities in older adults
sources.scope: Twenty-one community-dwelling older adults performed bodyweight forward and lateral step-ups onto a 21-centimeter platform with three-dimensional motion analysis and inverse-dynamics estimates of lower-extremity joint angles, moments, impulse, work, and power. The forward condition directly anchors the active platform height, brief bilateral top support, trail-foot return followed by lead-foot return to the lower floor, prohibition on trail-leg push-off or hopping, and hip-, knee-, and ankle-extension task; the older cohort and absence of muscle EMG or external load prevent generalization to arbitrary heights, loaded variants, continuous lead-foot-on-platform repetitions, or a muscle-magnitude ranking.

sources.title: Neuromuscular effects of dorsiflexor training with and without blood flow restriction
sources.scope: Seventeen healthy adults performed unilateral seated concentric-eccentric ankle dorsiflexion against a blue elastic band affixed to a foot board, both without and with thigh-cuff blood-flow restriction. The directly reported self-selected resting board position, individualized comfortable dorsiflexion stop, return until sole contact, and tibialis-anterior EMG anchor the non-occluded band exercise. The source does not establish fibularis-tertius or toe-extensor roles, a universal knee or ankle angle, comparable band load, a fixed external path, or a separate blood-flow-restriction exercise.

sources.title: Hip muscle activity during 3 side-lying hip-strengthening exercises in distance runners
sources.scope: Twenty healthy distance runners performed neutral side-lying hip abduction, side-lying abduction with external rotation, and clamshell exercise while gluteus medius, tensor fasciae latae, anterior hip flexors, and gluteus maximus surface EMG were recorded. The active neutral-abduction condition used a treatment table, a cuff weight equal to five percent of body mass just above the ankle, a flexed lower support leg, neutral sagittal hip posture, toes forward, a horizontal contact band at 35 degrees, and pressure biofeedback beneath the trunk inflated to 40 mmHg and maintained between 35 and 45 mmHg. Every analyzed repetition used that feedback; McBeth describes it as substitution control and cites prior work for its effect on gluteus-medius recruitment, but did not compare feedback with no feedback. The source does not support a no-feedback adaptation, one universal cuff load, gluteus-minimus credit, hypertrophy magnitude, or standing, machine, band, bodyweight-only, or rotated variants.

sources.title: EMG evaluation of hip adduction exercises for soccer players: implications for exercise selection in prevention and treatment of groin injuries
sources.scope: Forty healthy elite male soccer players performed eight hip-adduction exercises while bilateral adductor-longus plus gluteus-medius, rectus-abdominis, and external-oblique surface EMG were recorded. The reviewed elastic-band condition was a supported upright standing exercise with the band cuffed at the ankle, a straight working knee, toes forward, a maximal-abduction start, and the reported foot-relative medial endpoint. Gluteus medius reached 18 percent MVC on both measured sides in this condition and supports categorical hip-and-pelvis stabilization credit. The sagittal coordinate of the abducted start and the three-dimensional path were not reported; the posterior endpoint neither establishes a separate hip-extension prime action nor directly supports the catalog's mechanics-derived held-posterior adaptation. The source supports the topology, adductor-longus role, gluteus-medius stabilization, and rectus-abdominis/external-oblique trunk control, not internal-oblique measurement, gracilis ranking, comparable band load, or another support, posture, or resistance topology.

sources.title: Eccentric strengthening effect of hip-adductor training with elastic bands in soccer players: a randomised controlled trial
sources.scope: Thirty-four healthy sub-elite male soccer players were randomized to control or eight weeks of supervised full-range standing hip-adduction training with elastic bands while the upper body was fixed to a stationary object with both hands. Training progressed from three sets of fifteen-repetition maximum to three sets of ten and then eight, and produced a larger eccentric-strength increase than control. The sagittal coordinate of the abducted start and the three-dimensional path were not reported, so the study does not establish a separate hip-extension prime action or directly support the catalog's mechanics-derived held-posterior adaptation. It supports the bilateral stable-hand setup, a trainable dynamic band topology, and the eight-to-fifteen repetition range, not muscle-specific roles, a comparable external load, another band geometry, or a different posture.

sources.title: The effects of curl-up exercise in terms of posture and muscle contraction direction on muscle activity and thickness of trunk muscles
sources.scope: Fourteen healthy males performed concentric and eccentric curl-ups at 30, 60, and 90 degrees while rectus-abdominis, external-oblique, internal-oblique, and iliopsoas EMG plus transversus-abdominis ultrasound thickness were collected. Abdominal activity decreased as the curl-up angle increased, directly anchoring the active 30-degree dynamic range and measured abdominal participation. The study does not establish a comparable external load, bodyweight fraction, universal arm or lower-limb geometry, zero iliopsoas activity, a categorical numeric role split, full sit-ups, loaded or unstable variants, rotation, lateral flexion, or higher-angle roster records.

sources.title: Core Muscle Activity, Exercise Preference, and Perceived Exertion during Core Exercise with Elastic Resistance versus Machine
sources.scope: Seventeen healthy untrained men performed three controlled left-to-right torso-twist repetitions at individually determined ten-repetition-maximum loads using elastic resistance and a horizontal seated Technogym machine. The machine condition directly anchors the left-rotated start, feet behind ankle rollers, hands on shoulder-height handles, the photographed shoulder-pad lever interface, controlled maximal rightward torso-rotation endpoint, return, and rectus-abdominis, bilateral external-oblique, and bilateral erector-spinae EMG context. Machine-condition pelvic kinematics were neither stated as stationary nor measured, so the source does not prove zero pelvic motion, internal-oblique activity, a universal range or stack load, chronic training outcomes, upper-limb roles, a mirrored record, or another topology.

sources.title: The relevance of increasing resistance on trunk muscle activity during seated axial rotation
sources.scope: Thirty healthy adults performed dynamic seated axial rotation in a Tergumed training device at 30, 50, and 70 percent of maximum mean force while fourteen abdominal and back muscle sites were measured. Internal oblique reached approximately 30 percent MVIC at the lowest load, while external oblique and the examined back muscles reached approximately 60 percent, and activity increased with resistance. The study supports dynamic internal-and-external-oblique participation in resisted seated rotation, not equivalence to the active Technogym topology, its exact contacts, a categorical numeric role partition, a universal range or load, zero pelvic motion, or chronic training outcomes.

sources.title: Trunk muscle activity during bridging exercises on and off a Swiss ball
sources.scope: Eleven resistance-trained men performed a stable-floor prone bridge with feet and forearms contacting the floor, elbows below the shoulders, upper arms perpendicular to the floor, neutral spine-and-leg alignment, and a five-second isometric collection while rectus-abdominis, external-oblique, internal-oblique, and L3 erector-spinae surface EMG was recorded. It directly supports the stable fixture and conservative trunk-role envelope, not a universal endurance prescription, bodyweight load fraction, sex-independent magnitude, shoulder or hip role ranking, unstable or suspended variants, or hypertrophy.

sources.title: Is the Side Bridge Test Valid and Reliable for Assessing Trunk Lateral Flexor Endurance in Recreational Female Athletes?
sources.scope: Recreationally active young women performed a preferred-side floor side bridge supported by the forearm, elbow, and feet with shoulder and elbow at 90 degrees, extended legs, the non-preferred foot in front, the free hand on the contralateral shoulder, straight shoulder-hip-feet alignment, and a hold to exhaustion. All eight EMG sites—rectus abdominis, external and internal oblique, rectus femoris, gluteus medius, deltoid, latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae—were recorded on the preferred support side. The source supports the exact fixture and measured regional demand, but not bilateral measurement; shoulder fatigue and anthropometry make it a multi-joint task rather than a pure or cross-user-normalized lateral-flexor test, and it does not resolve left/right credit inside bilateral mesh aggregates or directly measure quadratus lumborum.

sources.title: Effect of Body Position and Support Surface on the Postural Control Challenge During the Pallof Press Exercise: A Smartphone Accelerometer-Based Study
sources.scope: Twelve physically active adults performed fifteen-second isometric Pallof conditions with both hands at shoulder height, elbows extended, arms perpendicular to the body, a horizontal elastic band attached to a side pulley, body-mass-bracketed dynamometer-standardized lateral force, and sacral smartphone acceleration. It directly supports the feet-together standing-on-floor topology and postural challenge, not muscle roles, self-selected load equivalence, a dynamic press, cable-stack load, or a hypertrophy outcome.

sources.title: Neuromuscular activation following anti-movement and dynamic core training: a randomized controlled comparative study
sources.scope: Thirty-six recreationally trained men were randomized to anti-movement, traditional-dynamic, or control groups for two sessions weekly over six weeks. The anti-movement program used thirty-second isometric sets and included stable prone plank, lateral plank, and standing Pallof hold among several exercises and progressions. It supports trainability and the thirty-second product detent, not a per-exercise causal adaptation, muscle-role hierarchy, exact Juan-Recio Pallof geometry, or one exercise's isolated EMG response.

sources.title: The Quantification of Muscle Activation During the Loaded Carry Movement Pattern
sources.scope: Healthy college-aged participants completed randomized, time- and intensity-matched plank, farmer-carry, suitcase-carry, farmer-hold, and suitcase-hold conditions. The carries covered 25 meters with two equally weighted dumbbells bilaterally or one right-hand dumbbell unilaterally; rectus abdominis, external oblique, longissimus, and multifidus surface EMG was measured bilaterally. It directly supports the carry-versus-hold boundary, paired-versus-single dumbbell topology, and categorical trunk-control envelope, but not side-specific product highlighting, lower-limb roles, a universal external-load percentage, or the catalog duration and weight seeds.

sources.title: Low back loads while walking and carrying: comparing the load carried in one hand or in both hands
sources.scope: Six healthy men with complete data walked while carrying 5-to-30-kilogram buckets either in the right hand or evenly across both hands. Bilateral rectus-abdominis, internal- and external-oblique, latissimus, thoracic-erector, and lumbar-erector EMG, full-body three-dimensional kinematics, force plates, and an anatomically detailed lumbar model directly establish the one-versus-two-hand loading distinction and greater asymmetric trunk demand. The source does not support dumbbell-specific upper-limb roles, side-specific catalog highlighting, duration seeds, or a claim that gait-related spinal motion is absent.

sources.title: The Gluteus Medius Vs. Thigh Muscles Strength Ratio and Their Relation to Electromyography Amplitude During a Farmer's Walk Exercise
sources.scope: Sixteen resistance-trained men completed 8-meter dumbbell farmer-walk trials; the analyzed condition used 75 percent of each participant's six-repetition-maximum load, upright-trunk and retracted-shoulder instructions, and natural lower-limb technique. Bilateral gluteus-medius, vastus-medialis, vastus-lateralis, and biceps-femoris surface EMG plus hip-and-knee three-dimensional kinematics support the bilateral dumbbell fixture and categorical gluteus-medius and knee-control envelope. The study measured only four muscles, stratified activation by strength ratios, and does not establish suitcase roles, fixed gait technique, or catalog load and duration seeds.

sources.title: Heavier- and lighter-load isolated lumbar extension resistance training produce similar strength increases, but different perceptual responses, in healthy males and females
sources.scope: Twenty-six asymptomatic adults trained isolated dynamic lumbar extension once weekly for six weeks on the MedX lumbar-extension machine at either 80 or 50 percent maximum voluntary contraction. The directly described restraint system fixed the thighs and distal femurs, supported the feet, and used a posterior-pelvis pad to prevent pelvic lift and rotation while permitting lumbar motion from the machine's 72-degree full-flexion reference to 0-degree full extension. Repetitions used at least two seconds of extension, a one-second full-extension hold, and at least four seconds of controlled return. The study did not record EMG. It supports the exact isolated fixture and lumbar-extensor training outcome, not a visible erector-spinae or multifidus surface, muscle-subdivision ranking, a universal stack load, another machine, unsupported back extension, hip extension, or pain treatment advice.

sources.title: Neuromuscular Evaluation of Trunk-Training Exercises
sources.scope: Ten healthy exercise-familiar adults performed nine repetitions of twelve standardized trunk exercises while a trunk goniometer and surface EMG from rectus abdominis, external oblique, rectus femoris, middle trapezius, erector spinae at T12 and L3, gluteus maximus, and medial hamstrings were recorded. The active lateral-flexion condition was side-lying with the upper foot crossed over the lower leg and that crossed foot externally fixed while the upper body lifted to a 30-degree trunk-elevation endpoint. The source does not identify the fixation device, and the endpoint is not a segmental lumbar lateral-flexion angle. It directly supports that dynamic fixture, endpoint, external-oblique emphasis, and erector-spinae and rectus-abdominis coactivation context. It did not measure quadratus lumborum, internal oblique, or multifidus; directly establish position-held hip or pelvis motion; rank the catalog's combined oblique region against quadratus lumborum; or support an unfixed-leg side bend, external loading, a comparable bodyweight fraction, side-specific volume, or another lateral-flexion topology. The active record's 10-repetition seed and 8-to-15 recommendation are product defaults, not source prescriptions.

sources.title: EMG activities of the quadratus lumborum and erector spinae muscles during flexion-relaxation and other motor tasks
sources.scope: Seven healthy adults underwent ultrasound-guided fine-wire EMG of quadratus lumborum and deep lateral and superficial medial erector spinae during multiple motor tasks. Quadratus lumborum and deep lateral erector spinae reached their highest observed activity during maximal ipsilateral trunk flexion in side-lying with the legs supported. Combined with Konrad's dynamic fixed-leg side-lying fixture and Christophy's lumbar mechanics, this provides a triangulated, condition-matched basis for categorical quadratus-lumborum participation; it does not directly measure the active 30-degree repetitions, establish a numeric primary-secondary partition, support side-specific product credit, or generalize to standing loaded side bends.

sources.title: Anatomy and biomechanics of quadratus lumborum
sources.scope: Detailed fascicular dissection in six embalmed cadavers informed a quantitative force-equivalent model of quadratus lumborum. The model established possible lumbar extensor and lateral-bending moments, each no greater than ten percent of the corresponding erector-spinae and multifidus contribution. It supports both modest actions in the exact quadratus-lumborum capability profile, not an exercise role, a primary ranking, side-specific product credit, an in-vivo recruitment magnitude, or substitution for the substantially larger lumbar-extensor system.

sources.title: Variation of rotation moment arms with hip flexion
sources.scope: Rotation moment arms for eighteen compartments across gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus plus iliopsoas, piriformis, quadratus femoris, obturator internus, and obturator externus at 0, 20, 45, 60, and 90 degrees of hip flexion in four cadaveric specimens, with comparison to a three-dimensional model. It directly supports posture-conditioned action directions and adverse whole-region aggregation boundaries. It did not measure either gemellus and does not establish exercise-specific recruitment, categorical roles, or contribution magnitudes.

sources.title: Activation of the gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and tensor fascia lata muscles during hip internal and external rotation exercises at three hip flexion postures
sources.scope: Twenty-one participants performed maximal isometric internal- and external-rotation efforts at 0, 45, and 90 degrees of hip flexion while force and surface EMG from upper and lower gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, and tensor fasciae latae were recorded. It supports posture-sensitive recruitment and condition-matched internal-rotation participation at 90 degrees, not a dynamic fixture, deep-rotator policy, net torque direction for a whole muscle, or a numeric cross-muscle role ranking.

sources.title: Test-Retest and Inter-Rater Reliability of a Rotary Axis Encoder-Flywheel System for the Assessment of Hip Rotation Exercises
sources.scope: Twenty-nine physically active adults performed separate dynamic high-intensity hip internal- and external-rotation repetitions with a rotary-encoder flywheel while seated on a 75-centimeter table with both hips and knees at 90 degrees, feet suspended, hands crossed, pelvis neutral, an ankle brace connected to the cable, distal-femur restraint, and two belts across the anterior superior iliac spines. It directly supports the loadable dynamic fixture, resistance interface, repetition semantics, and non-comparable force and power boundary. It measured no muscle activity and does not establish individual-muscle roles.

sources.title: The anatomy and function of the gluteus minimus muscle
sources.scope: Dissection of sixteen fresh-cadaver hips plus a plastic-bone mechanical model described gluteus-minimus attachments, capsular stabilization, abduction, and position- and fiber-dependent rotation. It supports a distinct unvisualized region and rejects unconditional aggregate rotation, not exercise-specific involvement or a categorical training-role ranking.

sources.title: Comparison of External Rotation Torque of Short External Rotator Muscles in Hip Flexion Position
sources.scope: Fifteen fresh-frozen hips informed PCSA-scaled muscle-string external-rotation torque estimates for piriformis, obturator internus, the obturator-internus and gemelli conjoined tendon, and obturator externus from 0 through 105 degrees of flexion. It supports position-specific deep-rotator capability and relative mechanical capacity at 30 degrees, not neural recruitment or an exercise role by itself. Quadratus femoris was explicitly excluded and receives no ranking from this source.

sources.title: Primary functions of the quadratus femoris and obturator externus muscles indicated from lengths and moment arms measured in mobilized cadavers
sources.scope: Wire paths simulating dissected quadratus femoris and obturator externus were measured in three mobilized cadaver hips at 15-degree flexion increments with rotation, abduction, adduction, and combined positions. Internal rotation lengthened both muscles and supports their possible external-rotation action, while the study's broader findings emphasize additional extension, flexion, and adduction functions. It does not measure exercise recruitment, rank quadratus femoris within the active band fixture, or license a single undifferentiated deep-rotator aggregate.

sources.title: The Foot Orthoses versus Hip eXercises (FOHX) trial for patellofemoral pain: a protocol for a randomized clinical trial to determine if foot mobility is associated with better outcomes from foot orthoses
sources.scope: The FOHX protocol specifies a progressive resisted hip-exercise program. Its external-rotation fixture is unilateral and supine with both hips supported at 30 degrees over a wedge, the knee stabilized by a therapist, an elastic band attached at the ankle and held by the therapist, and motion from neutral to the midpoint of available external rotation at an approximately 10-to-12-repetition-maximum resistance. It directly supports that topology and progression, not a deep-muscle role hierarchy, exact band force, generic self-anchored band work, or another hip-flexion posture.

sources.title: Does foot mobility affect the outcome in the management of patellofemoral pain with foot orthoses versus hip exercises? A randomised clinical trial
sources.scope: A two-site randomized clinical trial assigned 218 adults with patellofemoral pain to foot orthoses or the FOHX progressive resisted hip-exercise program, confirming implementation of the four-week, twelve-session program and assessing outcomes at twelve weeks. It supports program implementation and trainability, not an isolated causal effect of the external-rotation exercise, individual-muscle recruitment, a role hierarchy, or treatment advice for the general catalog user.

sources.title: Surface Electromyographic Analysis of the Lower Trapezius Muscle During Exercises Performed Below Ninety Degrees of Shoulder Elevation in Healthy Subjects
sources.scope: Fifteen healthy adults performed five repetitions each of unilateral elastic-band scapular retraction with the shoulder held at 80 degrees of flexion and unilateral overhead-band scapular depression with the arm beside the torso. The band began just taut, resistance was adjusted to a subject-reported moderate five-repetition effort, each concentric and eccentric phase lasted approximately two seconds, and repetitions were separated by five seconds. Surface EMG directly measured upper, middle, and lower trapezius plus serratus anterior participation. The study prescribed the target scapular motions but did not measure three-dimensional scapular kinematics, rhomboids, pectoralis minor, joint torque, or a cross-muscle force hierarchy.

sources.title: Evaluation of Isokinetic Force Production and Associated Muscle Activity in the Scapular Rotators During a Protraction-Retraction Movement in Overhead Athletes With Impingement Symptoms
sources.scope: Nineteen overhead athletes completed reciprocal maximal concentric protraction and retraction on a Biodex System 3 with the torso strapped, arm horizontal in the scapular plane, humerus neutral, and elbow extended. The study directly measured isokinetic force and upper-, middle-, and lower-trapezius plus serratus-anterior EMG, supporting middle- and lower-trapezius participation during the retraction phase. It is supplemental role evidence only: the reciprocal assessment is not the active one-way band-retraction fixture, upper-trapezius and serratus activity is co-contraction rather than proof of retraction production, and the study measured neither rhomboids nor three-dimensional scapular coupling.

sources.title: Various Shrug Exercises Can Change Scapular Kinematics and Scapular Rotator Muscle Activities in Subjects With Scapular Downward Rotation Syndrome
sources.scope: Seventeen participants with scapular downward-rotation syndrome performed two bilateral shrug trials while holding 30 degrees of frontal-plane shoulder abduction, maintained the individual maximum-height target for five seconds, and then returned slowly. The stabilization condition used wrist guides, individualized target bars, inclinometer-confirmed arm position, and investigator stabilization of the chin and prominent thoracic spinous process. Surface EMG was collected during the five-second isometric phase, and digital-inclinometer scapular upward-rotation angle was measured immediately after each exercise condition rather than continuously through the repetition. The greater post-condition upward-rotation angle supports a coupled elevation-plus-upward-rotation variant in the existing scapular-elevation family, not a dynamic angle trace, a pure or separately owned upward-rotation family, or an unrestricted loaded shrug.

sources.title: Pulling Exercises for Strength Training and Rehabilitation: Movements and Loading Conditions
sources.scope: Fifteen healthy adults performed standing low-cable straight-bar upright rows on a Technogym Ercolina Rehab at ten and twenty-five percent of bodyweight for two sets of eight repetitions. Instructions fixed a shoulder-width stance, upright engaged torso, vertical bar path, elbows slightly above the hands, an elbows-at-shoulder-height endpoint, and controlled return. Twenty-two-camera motion capture and a cable load cell directly support the fixture, mixed sagittal-plus-frontal shoulder path, elbow flexion, and non-held spinal behavior. No scapular coordinate system or EMG was used, and the Rab XYZ shoulder decomposition becomes indeterminate near ninety degrees of abduction; the source therefore does not establish numeric humeral components, axial rotation, scapular actions, or muscle rankings.

sources.title: Effect of Grip Width on Electromyographic Activity During the Upright Row
sources.scope: Sixteen resistance-trained men performed two barbell upright-row repetitions at fifty, one hundred, and two hundred percent of biacromial grip breadth using one common load equal to eighty-five percent of the shoulder-width condition's one-repetition maximum. Surface EMG directly measured anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoid, upper and middle trapezius, biceps brachii, and latissimus dorsi. It supports categorical upright-row participation and within-muscle grip-width effects only; raw cross-channel amplitudes do not rank muscles, the barbell protocol does not authorize a cable grip-width claim, and EMG does not establish joint or scapular actions.

sources.title: External Handheld Loads Affect Scapular Elevation and Upward Rotation During Shoulder Elevation Tasks
sources.scope: Fifty healthy adults performed dumbbell elevation in the scapular plane from thirty to one hundred twenty degrees under unloaded and individualized external-load conditions while three-dimensional motion capture measured scapular elevation and upward rotation. The study supports persistence of coupled upward rotation during loaded arm elevation and reports only small load-related changes. It did not measure posterior tilt, muscle activity, or an upright-row fixture, so it cannot independently assign upright-row roles, scapular elevation, or fixed coupling magnitudes.

sources.title: Differential Activation of Psoas Major and Rectus Femoris During Active Straight Leg Raise to End Range
sources.scope: Nine healthy men performed a supine active straight-leg raise through concentric motion to each participant's active end range, an end-range hold, and eccentric lowering. Fine-wire psoas-major EMG plus surface rectus-femoris, rectus-abdominis, external-oblique, and internal-oblique/transversus-abdominis EMG directly support psoas-dominant late-range hip-flexor participation, rectus-femoris participation, and abdominal control of trunk and pelvic movement. The study does not establish a universal endpoint angle, cadence, hold duration, external load, zero pelvic or spinal motion, iliacus-specific magnitude, or roles for sartorius, tensor fasciae latae, or adductors.

sources.title: Kinetic and Kinematic Differences Between Deadlifts and Goodmornings
sources.scope: Thirteen healthy participants performed eight barbell good-morning repetitions with an added load equal to twenty-five percent of body mass, shoulder-width slightly externally rotated feet, an upright start, equal self-selected lowering and raising speeds, deliberate core tension, and a cue to avoid lumbar flexion. Three-dimensional motion capture and force plates directly measured large hip excursion, material pelvis-lumbar and lumbar-thoracic excursion, and small nondefining knee motion. The procedure and standardized instruction differ between upper-trapezius and rear-deltoid bar-site wording, so the catalog preserves only a coarse posterior-shoulder/upper-back placement. The study did not measure EMG, prescribe universal segment angles, or authorize Romanian-deadlift, stiff-leg-deadlift, floor-pull, unilateral, or externally supported variants; muscle roles are conservative mechanics-and-anatomy assignments rather than measured rankings.

sources.title: Joint Kinetics and Kinematics During Common Lower Limb Rehabilitation Exercises
